question: What is CRISPR gene editing, and what was the first CRISPR-based therapy to be approved?

answer.text:
**CRISPR gene editing** is a way to change DNA at a chosen location. In CRISPR-Cas9, a guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence. Cas9 cuts the DNA, and the cell’s own repair process can be used to disable a gene or change its sequence. ([medlineplus.gov](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/understanding/genomicresearch/genomeediting/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))

**Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel)** was the first CRISPR-based therapy approved anywhere in the world. The UK authorized it on **November 16, 2023**, for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia. The U.S. FDA approved it for sickle cell disease on **December 8, 2023**, and for transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia on **January 16, 2024**. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/mhra-authorises-world-first-gene-therapy-that-aims-to-cure-sickle-cell-disease-and-transfusion-dependent-thalassemia?utm_source=openai))

Casgevy works by editing a patient’s own blood-forming stem cells outside the body, then returning them to the patient so they can produce red blood cells with more fetal hemoglobin. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/mhra-authorises-world-first-gene-therapy-that-aims-to-cure-sickle-cell-disease-and-transfusion-dependent-thalassemia?utm_source=openai))
